How much to charge to stripe a parking lot

Property managers type that phrase when they want a number they can put on a work order. Striping contractors hear the same phrase as “match last year’s $8-a-stall special.” The two jobs those words describe are not the same.

Price the lines, the ADA hash, and the coats

A per-stall special cannot see the lot

A 50-stall retail restripe with faded 4-inch lines is mostly paint and a short crew day. The same stall count with six ADA stalls, hashed access aisles, twenty-four arrows, a fire lane, two coats, and a new string-line layout is a different Saturday. Stall count is a convenient unit. It is a poor cost driver.

Adjacent 90-degree stalls share a side line, so a typical starting figure is about 18 lineal feet of 4-inch paint per stall — not the lot’s square footage, and not “one stall equals one unit of work.” ADA stalls add hashed aisle line that never shows up in that 18 feet.

What actually moves the bid

  1. Restripe versus new layout. Following existing paint is not measuring, snapping a line, and painting a first layout. New-layout hours sit on every stall, not just the extras.
  2. ADA hash, symbols, and signs. Treating an ADA stall as a regular stall is how an $8 special underprices the aisle. The extra is gallons and hours, not a courtesy.
  3. Stencils and fire lanes. Arrows, stop bars, crosswalks, and “FIRE LANE” footage are solid fill or extra lineal feet. They do not come free with the stall count.
  4. Coats. Two coats is almost another paint ticket. It is not another mobilization. Pricing it as either free or “double the job” is how the margin disappears.
  5. Night work. A closed lot after hours is a labor premium on the same scope, not a different stall count.

A walk-away number

Load the wage (employer taxes, workers’ compensation, and time off). Add paint, ADA signs, and mobilization. Put overhead on that direct cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below it the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Margin is a share of the customer’s number, not a markup on cost.

What this is not

This is not a MUTCD plan, an ADA determination, a traffic-engineering stamp, a pavement-condition report, or a quote you should send without checking your own tickets. Sealcoating, asphalt paving, gravel, and concrete pours are different trades with different units. Use the parking lot striping bid calculator to run the arithmetic on your rates.

Common questions

How much to charge to stripe a parking lot?

Price the lineal feet of stall line, the extra ADA hash, the stencils, the coats, and whether the layout is new or a restripe. A flat per-stall number hides those extras.

Why is a 50-stall new layout more than a 50-stall restripe?

A restripe follows existing paint. A new layout adds string-line hours per stall, and ADA aisles, arrows, and fire lanes add paint that stall count does not show.

Does a second coat double the price?

A second coat is almost another paint ticket, not another setup day. Labor for the second coat is typically a fraction of first-coat paint labor.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, traffic-engineering, or ADA advice. Verify every figure before you bid.

vs-a-flat-8-per-stall-special.html.text:
← Parking Lot Striping Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $8-a-stall special

“$8 a stall” or “$400 for a 50-space lot” is not a price for parking-lot striping — it is a price for one specific layout, ADA count, and coat count, quietly applied to every lot that calls in.

What a flat price per stall is

A flat rate per stall is the fastest way to quote a striping job: multiply the stall count by a number and read off a price. It is the number a property manager holding last year's invoice or a competitor's flyer will call and ask you to match, whatever their lot actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a faded restripe following existing paint, a couple of ADA stalls, a handful of arrows, one coat, no fire lane — and then reused for every lot afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter standard and ADA stall counts, arrows, stop bars, crosswalks, handicap symbols, fire-lane and curb footage, restripe versus new layout, coats, and night work, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the layout, the ADA aisles, the stencils, and the coats separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this lot, not a generic one.

What a flat price per stall doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/stall whether the job follows existing paint or needs a full string-line new layout, even though new-layout hours sit on every stall, not just the extras. Prices restripe versus new layout separately, so a new-layout job costs more than a restripe of the same stall count.
Has no line for ADA hash aisles and signs, regardless of whether the lot carries two ADA stalls or six. Prices ADA hash line, symbols, and signs separately by count, so an ADA-heavy lot costs more than one with few accessible stalls.
Has no line for arrows, stop bars, crosswalks, fire-lane footage, curb paint, or a second coat, regardless of how much the job needs. Prices each extra separately — stencils, fire lane, curb, and second-coat labor — so a fully-marked lot costs more than a bare restripe.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-stall rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two lots, the same stall-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($28/hr crew wage, 28% burden, 15% overhead, a 25% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $22.54/stall rateGap
50-stall retail restripe, 1 coat, 2 ADA, 8 arrows — the cheap special the rate is set from$1,126.98 bid price; $845.24 break-even cost$1,126.98 (exactly $22.54/stall — this rate is fit to this job)No gap on the job the rate was built on.
120-stall new layout, 2 coats, 6 ADA, 24 arrows, 2 crosswalks, fire lane, night work — where the special loses$6,110.34 bid price; $4,582.75 break-even cost$2,704.76The rate quotes $1,877.99 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $3,405.58 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $22.54/stall rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the retail-restripe preset, divided by that preset's own stall count. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the new-layout job, it counts only the stalls and never sees the string-line hours, the extra ADA aisles, the fire lane, the second coat, or the night premium at all. Run your own lot's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-stall rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one lot it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per stall get a parking-lot striping bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is restripe versus new layout, ADA hash aisles and signs, stencils and fire-lane footage, and coats -- not a blended stall count. A 120-stall new layout with ADA hash, arrows, a fire lane, and two coats is doing several jobs a 50-stall restripe never touches, none of which scale with stall count the way a per-stall rate assumes.

What does a flat price per stall usually leave out entirely?

New-layout measuring and string-line hours, ADA hash aisle line and signs, arrows and stop-bar stencils, crosswalks, fire-lane and curb footage, and a second coat. A faded restripe with a couple of ADA stalls is doing far less than a new layout with a fire lane and two coats -- and a per-stall number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates: a 50-stall retail restripe prices at $1,126.98, or $22.54 a stall. Applying that same $22.54 rate to a 120-stall new layout with ADA hash, arrows, a fire lane, and two coats quotes $2,704.76, which is $1,877.99 below that job's own $4,582.75 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $3,405.58 below the calculator's own $6,110.34 bid price.

Is a flat price per stall ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- a restripe, one coat, few ADA stalls, no fire lane -- a per-stall rate can land close, and on this calculator's own restripe preset it is exactly the rate that job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which lot it was built on and neither does the estimator until layout, ADA, stencils, and coats are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes stall counts, ADA aisles, stencils, fire-lane and curb footage, layout, and coats, plus the labor hours, paint cost, and wage you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-stall rate skips, not a market survey.

vs-saasphalt.html.text:
← Parking Lot Striping Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. SaaSphalt

Two different shapes: SaaSphalt runs an asphalt contractor's estimating, scheduling, invoicing and books across every crew. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one lot cost, given its stalls, fire lane, coats, and paint, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

SaaSphalt is estimating, scheduling and invoicing software for asphalt contractors, with a module aimed at line-striping work and an integration with QuickBooks, described as customisable to the way a given contractor works. It is sold as an ongoing account for a business, covering the paving, sealcoating and striping sides of a company rather than one trade in isolation. SaaSphalt's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's plan names or dollar figures, so none is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — asphalt-contractor business software, sold as an ongoing account — are stated, and no dollar amount for SaaSphalt appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what SaaSphalt does. It does not schedule a crew, raise an invoice, sync to your books, or keep a customer record on a server. It takes one lot's standard and ADA stall counts, handicap symbols, fire lane and curb paint footage, crosswalks, stop bars, arrows and signs, the number of coats, paint coverage and gallons, crew hours, loaded wage and payroll burden, mobilisation and travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the lot loses money — plus side-by-side comparisons of coats, layout and ADA count, a check of whether a price already on the table clears the floor, and a printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run an asphalt company and need estimating, scheduling, invoicing, and QuickBooks in one system across paving, sealcoating, and striping crews.SaaSphalt, or a comparable asphalt platform — running a whole company is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this one lot, given its stall count, fire lane, and curb footage, before I quote it?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
What does a second coat actually cost me on this specific lot?This calculator's coat comparison, priced from the same measurements rather than a rule of thumb.
How much do the ADA stalls and handicap symbols add over plain stalls?This calculator's separate ADA stall, symbol, and layout comparison lines.
Is the number the property manager is pushing me to still above my walk-away cost once paint and mobilisation are counted?This calculator's compare-to-proposed-price check.
How does the math behind a striping bid actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. SaaSphalt is used through a business account.

Most striping contractors get different value from each: SaaSphalt (or a comparable asphalt platform) for running estimates, schedules, invoices and books across a whole company, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one lot should cost before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off — which matters standing on a lot with a tape measure.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or SaaSphalt?

They do different jobs, and a striping business of any size may end up using both. SaaSphalt is estimating, scheduling and invoicing software for asphalt contractors, with a module aimed at line-striping work and an integration with QuickBooks, and it is described as customisable to the way a given contractor works. It is sold as an ongoing account for a company. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from standard and ADA stall counts, handicap symbols, fire lane and curb paint footage, crosswalks, stop bars, arrows, signs, the number of coats, paint coverage and gallons, crew hours, loaded wage and payroll burden, mobilisation and travel, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the lot loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A contractor already running estimates, schedules, invoices and books across paving, sealcoating and striping crews is better served by SaaSphalt or a comparable asphalt platform; a striper who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one lot should cost before opening a business system is in the right place here.

Can it compare one coat against two before I bid?

Yes, and that comparison is the reason the coat count is its own input rather than folded into a rate. A second coat roughly doubles the paint and adds crew hours without adding a single stall, so the two bids diverge by an amount that depends on the lot's own mix of stalls, fire lane, and curb. The calculator prices both from the same measurements, alongside comparisons of layout and ADA stall count, so the question a property manager asks — what does the better-looking job actually cost me — has a number rather than a guess. Each variant is checked against the same walk-away price, so a discount offered on the two-coat job cannot quietly fall below cost.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by SaaSphalt. SaaSphalt is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
